subject: PDC CLO 2
description: Hadoop ecosystem trade-offs — Hive, Pig, Kafka, Redis, Kubernetes, Spark.

questions.text: A consultancy is evaluating Hive vs. Pig for a new ETL workload. The team has strong SQL skills and the data is mostly structured. Another team has unstructured/semi-structured data and prefers a procedural pipeline style. Which assignment correctly reflects the strengths of each tool?
options: SQL team → Pig; procedural team → Hive
SQL team → Hive (declarative SQL-like queries on structured data); procedural team → Pig (data-flow language, handles structured/semi-structured/unstructured)
Both teams should use MapReduce directly because Hive and Pig are equivalent
SQL team → MapReduce; procedural team → Hive
Neither tool is suitable; only raw Java MapReduce can handle ETL
questions.shortExplanation: Hive fits SQL-style queries on structured data; Pig fits procedural pipelines on mixed data.
questions.explanation: Hive offers a declarative, SQL-like language called HiveQL that is friendly to teams already strong in SQL and working with cleanly structured tables. Pig instead offers Pig Latin, a step-by-step data-flow scripting language that handles structured, semi-structured, and unstructured data such as raw logs. So a team rich in SQL should pick Hive, while a team building procedural transformations on messy data should pick Pig. Both run on top of MapReduce or Tez but expose very different programming models. Writing raw Java MapReduce defeats the whole purpose of using a higher-level tool, and swapping Hive and Pig assigns each tool to the workload it is worst at, so those options are wrong.

questions.text: A platform team must choose between ACID semantics and BASE semantics for two workloads: (1) a banking transfer system that must never lose money or show partial updates, and (2) a global social-media timeline that prioritizes always being available even if some replicas lag. Which mapping is correct?
options: Banking → BASE; Social → ACID
Banking → ACID (strong consistency, transactional rollback); Social → BASE (eventual consistency, high availability)
Both should use BASE because ACID does not exist in distributed systems
Both should use ACID since BASE is unsafe
Banking → BASE because money is "soft state"
questions.shortExplanation: Use ACID for money-safe transactional workloads; use BASE for highly available, eventually consistent feeds.
questions.explanation: ACID systems give strong consistency and roll back on failure, which is what banking, trading, and wallet apps need so they never show a half-completed transfer. BASE systems trade strict consistency for high availability and partition tolerance, accepting that replicas may briefly disagree before converging. Social feeds, comments, and upvotes survive easily under BASE because users tolerate a few seconds of staleness in exchange for the system always being up. Mapping the workloads the other way around would risk losing money on the trading side or making the feed unavailable, and claiming ACID does not exist in distributed systems or BASE is always unsafe is simply wrong.

questions.text: A team has a 200 GB Hive table queried mainly for aggregations on 2–3 specific columns out of 50. They are choosing a storage format. Which is the BEST fit and why?
options: TEXTFILE — because text is the default and fastest
ORC or Parquet (columnar) — because columnar formats read only required columns, improving compression and analytical query speed
JSON — because JSON is splittable and column-oriented
Sequence file — because it always provides better compression than columnar formats
Avro — because Avro is purely columnar
questions.shortExplanation: ORC and Parquet are columnar — they read only the needed columns and compress them well.
questions.explanation: Analytical queries usually touch only a few columns out of many, so a columnar format stores values column-by-column on disk. This lets the engine skip the columns it does not need and read only the relevant ones, which cuts I/O dramatically. Columnar formats like ORC and Parquet also compress better because values within one column are usually similar in type and range. This is why they are the default choice for Hive analytical tables. TEXTFILE is plain text with no column skipping, JSON is row-oriented and not splittable everywhere, Sequence files are row-based binary, and Avro is row-oriented too, so none of them give the columnar speedup.

questions.text: A data lake holds shared raw CSV files that multiple teams query through Hive. The lead wants protection so that if one team accidentally drops the Hive table, the raw HDFS files survive. Which design choice is appropriate?
options: Use a managed table because managed tables protect underlying data
Use an external table because dropping it removes only metadata, not the underlying data
Disable HDFS writes entirely
Increase replication factor to 10
Use static partitioning to prevent deletions
questions.shortExplanation: External tables drop only their metadata; the underlying HDFS files are left intact.
questions.explanation: Hive has two table types. A managed table is fully owned by Hive, so dropping it deletes both the metadata and the data files. An external table only stores the schema in the metastore and points at existing HDFS data. If you drop an external table by mistake, the raw files in HDFS remain untouched and can be reattached or queried by another tool. This makes external tables the safe choice for shared raw data in a data lake. Managed tables, disabling HDFS writes, raising replication, or using static partitioning would either delete the data on drop or fail to protect it, so they do not solve the requirement.

questions.text: A company has yearly data of 100 GB partitioned by `country`. The team analyzes 99% of queries with `WHERE country='Pakistan'`. Their architect proposes partitioning the table by country. What is the PRIMARY benefit compared to a non-partitioned table?
options: Hive will scan the entire dataset every time, but format it nicely
Hive prunes partitions so only the `country=Pakistan` directory is scanned, dramatically reducing query time
The table data is automatically replicated to other regions
Hive will store data only in RAM
Partitioning has no effect on query time
questions.shortExplanation: Partitioning lets Hive skip directories and scan only the matching partition, cutting I/O.
questions.explanation: When a Hive table is partitioned by a column, each value of that column becomes a sub-directory in HDFS. A query that filters on the partition column lets Hive prune all the other directories and read only the files inside the matching partition. This can turn a full-table scan of hundreds of gigabytes into reading just one small folder, which speeds up the query massively. The price is more directories and more metastore entries. The other options either claim the full table is still scanned, that partitioning copies data across regions, or that data goes into RAM, which are not what HDFS partitioning does.

questions.text: After partitioning a Hive table by `country`, an engineer notices that two partitions hold 1 GB each, while one partition `country=USA` holds 90 GB. Queries on USA data are still slow because of skew. Which technique should the architect recommend ON TOP of partitioning?
options: Drop the table and use raw MapReduce
Apply bucketing within the partition using a hash function (e.g., `CLUSTERED BY (user_id) INTO N BUCKETS`) to further decompose data into manageable parts
Switch to OLTP processing
Use vertical scaling on a single node
Disable replication for the USA partition
questions.shortExplanation: Bucketing hashes rows inside a partition into N buckets to handle skew.
questions.explanation: Partitioning alone is not enough when one partition is much larger than the others, like a USA partition holding most of the data. Bucketing applies a hash function on a chosen column, such as user_id, and splits the partition into a fixed number of files called buckets. This breaks the skewed partition into smaller pieces that mappers and joins can handle in parallel. The CLUSTERED BY clause in Hive sets up bucketing on top of partitioning. Going back to raw MapReduce, switching to OLTP, scaling vertically, or disabling replication do not address skew at all and would only make the situation worse.

questions.text: A backend team must decide between Redis (in-memory cache) and a relational DB as the primary store for user profile data that is read 100,000 times/sec and rarely updated. Which trade-off analysis is correct?
options: Use the relational DB only because Redis offers no caching benefit
Use Redis as a cache layer in front of the DB — on a HIT it returns data with ~1 ms latency, on a MISS it reads from the DB and stores the result in Redis to absorb future reads
Replace the DB entirely with Redis since Redis guarantees full ACID durability
Use Redis only for writes, never reads
Caching is useful only for cold data that is never accessed
questions.shortExplanation: Put Redis in front of the DB: HIT returns in ~1 ms, MISS fetches from DB and stores back in Redis.
questions.explanation: Redis is an in-memory key-value store used as a caching layer. The app first checks Redis for the key. On a HIT, Redis returns the value in roughly a millisecond, saving the database from being hit. On a MISS, the app reads from the DB, writes the value into Redis (with an optional TTL), and returns the result. After enough warm-up, most reads are served from Redis and the DB load drops sharply, which is exactly what high read-rate, rarely-written data needs. Using only the DB ignores the cache benefit, replacing the DB with Redis loses real durability, write-only Redis defeats the read-cache purpose, and caching cold data wastes memory, so those options are wrong.

questions.text: A messaging team must decide between Apache Kafka and RabbitMQ. Workload A is high-throughput event streaming (log aggregation, real-time analytics) where consumers may replay history. Workload B is task offloading from a web server (PDF generation, sending emails) with rich routing rules via exchanges. Which assignment is BEST?
options: A → RabbitMQ; B → Kafka
A → Kafka (event streaming with retention and partitioning); B → RabbitMQ (message broker with flexible routing via exchanges)
Both should use Redis
Both should use Kubernetes
Both should use HDFS
questions.shortExplanation: Kafka for high-throughput streaming with replay; RabbitMQ for routed async task queues.
questions.explanation: Kafka is built around a partitioned, replicated, append-only log that retains messages and lets consumers replay history. This makes it the right choice for event streaming, log aggregation, and analytics pipelines that may need to rewind. RabbitMQ is a traditional message broker centered around exchanges, bindings, and queues, with flexible routing (direct, topic, fanout) for delivering tasks to specific workers, which is perfect for jobs like sending emails or generating PDFs. Swapping the two assigns each tool to its weak case, and Redis, Kubernetes, and HDFS are not messaging brokers at all, so they are not valid choices for either workload.

questions.text: A streaming pipeline ingests JSON and XML files into HDFS. The MapReduce performance is poor because the engine cannot parallelize splits well. Which property is most likely the cause?
options: JSON/XML are not naturally splittable on arbitrary byte boundaries (start/end tags must be respected), so MapReduce cannot easily split them across mappers
JSON/XML files cannot be stored in HDFS at all
HDFS automatically compresses JSON/XML, blocking parallelism
JSON/XML force the use of OLTP processing
Both formats require an external database to read
questions.shortExplanation: JSON and XML are not safely splittable on byte boundaries because tags must stay paired.
questions.explanation: MapReduce parallelizes work by cutting input files at fixed byte offsets and giving each chunk to a different mapper. JSON and XML rely on matching opening and closing tags or braces, so cutting in the middle of a record breaks the parser. Because MapReduce cannot safely split JSON and XML at any byte boundary, only one mapper ends up processing each file, which kills parallelism. Formats like Sequence, Avro, or ORC are designed to be splittable. The other options claim HDFS cannot store JSON, that it auto-compresses these formats, that they force OLTP, or that they need an external DB to read, none of which are true.

questions.text: A team must reduce I/O cost on a network-bound Hadoop job by enabling compression. They want a codec that is splittable so multiple mappers can still process the compressed file in parallel. Out of common Hadoop codecs (Gzip, Bzip2, Snappy, LZO indexed), which trade-off is correct?
options: Gzip is splittable and provides the highest compression ratio
Snappy gives high compression ratio but is the slowest
Bzip2 is splittable and offers high compression but is CPU-heavy/slow; Snappy and LZO are faster but Snappy is not splittable by default
All compression codecs in Hadoop are equally splittable
Compression always reduces CPU usage in all cases
questions.shortExplanation: Bzip2 is splittable but slow; Snappy and LZO are fast, but Snappy is not splittable by default.
questions.explanation: Choosing a Hadoop codec is a trade-off between compression ratio, speed, and splittability. Bzip2 compresses well and is splittable, so multiple mappers can attack the same file in parallel, but it is CPU-heavy and slow. Snappy and LZO are very fast and put low CPU pressure on the cluster, but plain Snappy cannot be split, so a single mapper must read the whole file. LZO can be made splittable with an index. Gzip is not splittable, Snappy does not have the highest ratio, not all codecs are equally splittable, and compression does not always reduce CPU, so those statements are wrong.

questions.text: Hive and Impala both query HDFS. A real-time BI dashboard needs sub-second responses on Hive-cataloged tables. Why might the architect choose Impala for this use case over Hive?
options: Hive uses long-running daemons on data nodes and is faster than Impala for interactive queries
Impala uses long-running daemons on data nodes and is designed for low-latency, interactive SQL — Hive is more suited to batch/ETL workloads via MapReduce/Tez
Hive supports only OLTP and not analytics
Impala does not use HDFS at all
Impala only works on a single machine
questions.shortExplanation: Impala runs long-lived daemons on data nodes for sub-second interactive SQL; Hive targets batch ETL.
questions.explanation: Hive compiles HiveQL into MapReduce or Tez jobs, which spend time starting and tearing down JVMs, so queries can take seconds to minutes. Impala instead runs its own long-running daemons on every DataNode that keep memory and metadata hot, executing queries directly without launching MapReduce. This makes Impala much faster for interactive BI dashboards that need sub-second responses, while Hive remains the better choice for long batch ETL. Saying Hive is faster, Hive supports only OLTP, Impala does not use HDFS, or Impala runs single-machine all misrepresent how each engine works.

questions.text: An analyst compares `JOIN` vs `COGROUP` in Pig. They have two relations and want pairs of tuples from both relations that match on a key. Which operator is the correct choice and why?
options: COGROUP — because it groups rows of one relation and ignores the other
JOIN — because it produces pairs of tuples from both relations that match the join condition, similar to SQL join
CROSS — because it returns the Cartesian product
FILTER — because it only filters one relation
FOREACH — because it iterates over one relation only
questions.shortExplanation: Pig JOIN returns matched pairs of tuples from two relations, like SQL inner join.
questions.explanation: When two Pig relations share a key and the analyst wants matched pairs of records, JOIN is the right operator. For each key value that exists in both relations, JOIN emits a row that combines the matching tuple from each side, exactly like a SQL inner join. The output is flat tuples that downstream FOREACH steps can use directly. JOIN is the standard way to combine related datasets in Pig. COGROUP keeps separate bags rather than producing matched pairs, CROSS produces a Cartesian product, FILTER works on one relation, and FOREACH only iterates, so none of them produce the SQL-join behavior the analyst wants.

questions.text: The same analyst now wants to group two relations on a common key but keep them as separate bags within each group (one bag per relation) so they can be processed independently per key. Which Pig operator is appropriate?
options: JOIN
CROSS
COGROUP — groups multiple relations by key and keeps them as separate bags per group (supports up to 127 relations)
FILTER
DUMP
questions.shortExplanation: COGROUP groups multiple relations by key and keeps each relation as a separate bag per group.
questions.explanation: COGROUP is Pig's way of grouping by a key across two or more relations while preserving the structure of each input. For every key value, the result has one row containing the key plus one separate inner bag for each input relation. This is different from JOIN, which would flatten matching tuples together, and it lets the analyst process each relation's tuples independently per key in a later FOREACH. COGROUP supports up to 127 relations. JOIN flattens the output, CROSS gives a Cartesian product, FILTER restricts a single relation, and DUMP only prints to console, so they do not produce the per-key separate-bag structure.

questions.text: A team is debating Static vs Dynamic partitioning in Hive. They have a huge raw file with no partition columns yet and want Hive to automatically create partitions based on a column value at load time. Which approach fits?
options: Static partitioning, because it requires the user to manually specify each partition
Dynamic partitioning (with `hive.exec.dynamic.partition.mode=nonstrict`), because partitions are derived from the source column values during load
Neither — Hive does not support partitioning
Bucketing only, because partitioning is not allowed on raw files
Use Pig instead since Hive cannot partition
questions.shortExplanation: Dynamic partitioning with nonstrict mode auto-creates partitions from source column values at load time.
questions.explanation: When a team has a raw unpartitioned file and wants Hive to derive partition values automatically during INSERT, dynamic partitioning is the answer. Setting `hive.exec.dynamic.partition.mode=nonstrict` allows all partition columns to be dynamic, so Hive reads each row, looks at the partition column value, and routes the row to the right partition directory on its own. Static partitioning, in contrast, forces the user to spell out each partition value by hand. Static partitioning needs manual values, claiming Hive does not partition is false, bucketing alone does not create partition directories, and Pig is not the solution either, so those alternatives do not fit.

questions.text: A retailer must decide between vertical scaling (upgrading a single big server to 1 TB RAM) and horizontal scaling (adding 50 commodity nodes). Their workload is highly parallel batch analytics on petabytes of data. Which trade-off analysis is correct?
options: Vertical scaling is best because it gives the lowest cost per terabyte for petabyte-scale analytics
Horizontal scaling fits this workload better — commodity nodes provide cost-effective parallelism, fault tolerance, and linear capacity growth; vertical scaling has hard hardware ceilings
Both options yield identical performance and cost characteristics
Vertical scaling is the only option supported by Hadoop
Horizontal scaling cannot tolerate node failures
questions.shortExplanation: Horizontal scaling adds commodity nodes for cost-effective parallelism and fault tolerance.
questions.explanation: For petabyte-scale, highly parallel batch analytics, the right move is horizontal scaling. Many commodity nodes share the work, the cluster grows almost linearly with data, and if one node fails the others keep the job alive thanks to replication. Vertical scaling soon hits a hard ceiling because a single server can hold only so much RAM, CPU, and disk, and the very largest machines are extremely expensive per terabyte. Vertical scaling at petabyte scale, identical cost claims, Hadoop-only-vertical claims, or denying horizontal fault tolerance all contradict how distributed Big Data clusters actually work.

questions.text: A senior engineer claims: "Compression and File Format are two separate concepts." Choose the option that BEST supports this claim in the context of Hive/HDFS.
options: They are the same thing — choosing a file format automatically determines the codec
File format defines on-disk layout (row/columnar, splittability) and schema; compression is an orthogonal codec choice (e.g., Snappy, Gzip) that may or may not preserve splittability
Compression formats cannot be applied to ORC or Parquet at all
File formats only matter for CSV; columnar formats need no decision about compression
Compression replaces the need for a file format entirely
questions.shortExplanation: File format defines layout and schema; compression is a separate codec choice on top of it.
questions.explanation: The on-disk file format such as ORC, Parquet, Avro, or TEXTFILE controls how rows or columns are stored, what schema is embedded, and whether the file is splittable. Compression, on the other hand, is a separate decision about which codec (Snappy, Gzip, Bzip2, Zlib) is applied to the bytes inside the file. The two decisions interact (some codecs break splittability) but they are orthogonal — you choose them independently for your workload. Saying format and codec are the same, that ORC and Parquet cannot be compressed, that formats only matter for CSV, or that compression replaces formats are all incorrect simplifications.

questions.text: A platform team is comparing how Kubernetes vs. a bare-VM deployment recover from a crashed application instance. Which Kubernetes feature directly addresses this failure mode?
options: Manual SSH into the failed VM and restart the process
Self-Healing — Kubernetes monitors application health and automatically restarts or replaces failed containers to maintain the declared desired state
Vertical scaling only
Kubernetes does not offer recovery; it relies on the developer to detect failures
The control plane shuts down the entire cluster
questions.shortExplanation: Kubernetes self-healing monitors containers and automatically restarts or replaces failed ones.
questions.explanation: Kubernetes constantly compares the cluster's actual state to the desired state declared in YAML manifests. If a container or Pod crashes, fails its liveness probe, or its node goes down, controllers automatically restart or reschedule a new instance to bring the system back to the declared replica count. This self-healing loop replaces the manual restart cycle that bare-VM deployments need and keeps services available with minimal human intervention. Manual SSH, vertical scaling only, leaving recovery to the developer, or shutting the cluster down on failure are all opposite of what Kubernetes self-healing actually does.

questions.text: An e-commerce platform is choosing where to apply Redis caching. Which is the BEST candidate dataset to cache, per the principles taught?
options: Highly volatile per-second order-book ticks that change every millisecond
Frequently accessed, relatively static reference data (e.g., product catalog read on every page) — shared across many requests with low write frequency
One-off admin reports run once a year
Random user-typed strings never reused
Data that must be ACID-transactional with strict isolation across nodes
questions.shortExplanation: The best Redis cache candidates are frequently read, mostly static, shared reference data.
questions.explanation: Caching gives the biggest win when the same value is requested many times across many users and rarely changes, such as a product catalog read on every page render. Such data has a high read-to-write ratio, fits easily in memory, and tolerates a short TTL. Caching very volatile data forces constant invalidation, caching one-off or random values gives no reuse, and trying to use Redis as a primary ACID store breaks consistency guarantees. Highly volatile ticks, annual one-off reports, random non-reused strings, and strict multi-document ACID workloads do not benefit from a cache and are therefore the wrong candidates.

questions.text: A team is comparing ROW-based (e.g., TEXTFILE, Sequence) vs COLUMN-based (e.g., ORC, Parquet) file formats for an analytic workload that filters a few columns out of 100. Which is correct?
options: Row-based formats outperform columnar formats for analytical queries because they read fewer columns
Columnar formats outperform row-based formats because they read only the columns referenced in the query, lowering I/O
Both perform identically because HDFS does not care about file layout
Row-based formats are always smaller after compression
Columnar formats cannot be queried with Hive
questions.shortExplanation: Columnar formats win for analytics because they read only the queried columns, cutting I/O.
questions.explanation: Analytical queries usually project just a few of the available columns. Row-based formats like TEXTFILE or Sequence store every row contiguously, so the engine must read all columns of every row even if it needs only a few. Columnar formats like ORC and Parquet store one column at a time on disk, so the engine can skip the columns the query does not need and read only the relevant ones, reducing I/O and improving compression at the same time. Row-based formats do not read fewer columns, performance is not identical between layouts, row-based compression is not always smaller, and columnar formats are fully Hive-queryable, so those claims are wrong.

questions.text: An architect compares Hadoop MapReduce and Apache Spark as Big Data engines. Hadoop writes intermediate results to HDFS between stages; Spark keeps intermediate data in memory across stages. Which statement BEST explains the operational implication?
options: Hadoop MapReduce typically incurs more I/O between stages because it materializes intermediate output to HDFS; Spark's in-memory model reduces I/O and accelerates iterative or multi-stage workloads
Spark cannot run on a Hadoop cluster
Both engines always have identical I/O profiles
Hadoop MapReduce keeps everything in memory, while Spark writes to HDFS
Spark requires no scheduler and runs only single-threaded
questions.shortExplanation: MapReduce writes to HDFS between stages; Spark keeps intermediate data in memory, reducing I/O.
questions.explanation: Hadoop MapReduce serializes the output of every stage back to HDFS before the next stage reads it again, which causes heavy disk and network I/O, especially for iterative or multi-stage jobs. Spark keeps intermediate RDDs and DataFrames in memory across stages, so iterative workloads such as machine learning or graph algorithms run much faster. Spark can still spill to disk when memory is short, and it can read input from HDFS, but the in-memory pipeline is its key advantage. Saying Spark cannot run on Hadoop, that both have identical I/O, that MapReduce keeps everything in memory, or that Spark needs no scheduler all contradict how these engines actually work.

Use static partitioning to block deletion

questions.text: A team compares Row-based (TEXTFILE, Sequence) vs Column-based (ORC, Parquet) formats for an analytical workload that filters only 9 columns out of 130. Which is correct?

Columnar wins because it reads only the columns referenced in the query, reducing I/O

Row-based formats are always smaller after compression
Columnar formats are not queryable from Hive

Spark cannot run on a Hadoop cluster
Both have identical I/O profiles
MapReduce keeps everything in memory; Spark writes to HDFS

COGROUP keeps separate bags rather than producing matched pairs, CROSS produces a Cartesian product, FILTER works on one relation, and FOREACH only iterates, so none of them produce the SQL-join behavior the analyst wants.

questions.text: The same analyst now wants two relations grouped by a common key but kept as SEPARATE bags within each group so each relation's tuples can be processed independently per key. Which Pig operator fits?
options: JOIN
CROSS
COGROUP — groups multiple relations by key, preserving separate bags per relation (supports up to 127 relations)
FILTER
DUMP
questions.shortExplanation: COGROUP groups multiple relations by key and keeps each relation as a separate bag per group.
questions.explanation: COGROUP is Pig's way of grouping by a key across two or more relations while preserving the structure of each input. For every key value, the result has one row containing the key plus one separate inner bag for each input relation. This is different from JOIN, which would flatten matching tuples together, and it lets the analyst process each relation's tuples independently per key in a later FOREACH. COGROUP supports up to 127 relations. JOIN flattens the output, CROSS gives a Cartesian product, FILTER restricts a single relation, and DUMP only prints to console, so they do not produce the per-key separate-bag structure.

questions.text: A Hive team chooses between Static and Dynamic partitioning. They have a large unpartitioned raw file and want Hive to auto-create partitions based on a column value at load time. Which approach is appropriate?
options: Static partitioning — requires manually specifying each partition value
Dynamic partitioning with `hive.exec.dynamic.partition.mode=nonstrict` — partitions are derived from source column values during the load
Hive does not support partitioning
Bucketing only — partitioning is forbidden on raw files
Use Pig because Hive cannot partition
questions.shortExplanation: Dynamic partitioning with nonstrict mode auto-creates partitions from source column values at load time.
questions.explanation: When a team has a raw unpartitioned file and wants Hive to derive partition values automatically during INSERT, dynamic partitioning is the answer. Setting `hive.exec.dynamic.partition.mode=nonstrict` allows all partition columns to be dynamic, so Hive reads each row, looks at the partition column value, and routes the row to the right partition directory on its own. Static partitioning, in contrast, forces the user to spell out each partition value by hand. Static partitioning needs manual values, claiming Hive does not partition is false, bucketing alone does not create partition directories, and Pig is not the solution either, so those alternatives do not fit.

questions.text: A retailer must choose between vertical scaling (one 8 TB RAM server) and horizontal scaling (150 commodity nodes) for highly parallel petabyte-scale batch analytics. Which analysis is correct?
options: Vertical scaling offers the lowest cost per TB at petabyte scale
Horizontal scaling fits — commodity nodes deliver cost-effective parallelism, fault tolerance, and near-linear capacity growth; vertical scaling has hard hardware ceilings
Both have identical cost and performance
Hadoop only supports vertical scaling
Horizontal scaling cannot survive node failures
questions.shortExplanation: Horizontal scaling adds commodity nodes for cost-effective parallelism and fault tolerance.
questions.explanation: For petabyte-scale, highly parallel batch analytics, the right move is horizontal scaling. Many commodity nodes share the work, the cluster grows almost linearly with data, and if one node fails the others keep the job alive thanks to replication. Vertical scaling soon hits a hard ceiling because a single server can hold only so much RAM, CPU, and disk, and the very largest machines are extremely expensive per terabyte. Vertical scaling at petabyte scale, identical cost claims, Hadoop-only-vertical claims, or denying horizontal fault tolerance all contradict how distributed Big Data clusters actually work.

questions.text: A senior engineer asserts: "Compression and File Format are two separate, orthogonal decisions in Hive/HDFS." Which statement BEST supports this claim?
options: They are the same — choosing a file format automatically dictates the codec
File format defines on-disk layout (row vs columnar, splittability, schema); compression is an orthogonal codec choice (Snappy, Gzip, Bzip2, Zlib) that may or may not preserve splittability
Compression cannot be applied to ORC or Parquet
File format only matters for CSV; columnar formats need no compression choice
Compression replaces the need for any file format
questions.shortExplanation: File format defines layout and schema; compression is a separate codec choice on top of it.
questions.explanation: The on-disk file format such as ORC, Parquet, Avro, or TEXTFILE controls how rows or columns are stored, what schema is embedded, and whether the file is splittable. Compression, on the other hand, is a separate decision about which codec (Snappy, Gzip, Bzip2, Zlib) is applied to the bytes inside the file. The two decisions interact (some codecs break splittability) but they are orthogonal — you choose them independently for your workload. Saying format and codec are the same, that ORC and Parquet cannot be compressed, that formats only matter for CSV, or that compression replaces formats are all incorrect simplifications.

questions.text: A platform team needs containerized applications to be detected and restarted automatically on failure — without human intervention. Which Kubernetes capability addresses this directly?
options: Manual SSH and process restart
Self-Healing — Kubernetes monitors application health and automatically restarts/replaces failed containers to maintain the declared desired state with minimal downtime
Vertical scaling only
Kubernetes provides no recovery; it depends on developers
Kubernetes shuts down the whole cluster on any failure
questions.shortExplanation: Kubernetes self-healing monitors containers and automatically restarts or replaces failed ones.
questions.explanation: Kubernetes constantly compares the cluster's actual state to the desired state declared in YAML manifests. If a container or Pod crashes, fails its liveness probe, or its node goes down, controllers automatically restart or reschedule a new instance to bring the system back to the declared replica count. This self-healing loop replaces the manual restart cycle that bare-VM deployments need and keeps services available with minimal human intervention. Manual SSH, vertical scaling only, leaving recovery to the developer, or shutting the cluster down on failure are all opposite of what Kubernetes self-healing actually does.

questions.text: An e-commerce team must choose what to cache in Redis. Which dataset is the BEST candidate per the caching principles taught?
options: Highly volatile order-book ticks changing every few milliseconds
Frequently accessed, mostly static reference data such as a product catalog — shared across many requests, low write rate
One-off annual admin reports
Random one-time user-typed strings never reused
Data requiring multi-document ACID transactions across nodes
questions.shortExplanation: The best Redis cache candidates are frequently read, mostly static, shared reference data.
questions.explanation: Caching gives the biggest win when the same value is requested many times across many users and rarely changes, such as a product catalog read on every page render. Such data has a high read-to-write ratio, fits easily in memory, and tolerates a short TTL. Caching very volatile data forces constant invalidation, caching one-off or random values gives no reuse, and trying to use Redis as a primary ACID store breaks consistency guarantees. Highly volatile ticks, annual one-off reports, random non-reused strings, and strict multi-document ACID workloads do not benefit from a cache and are therefore the wrong candidates.

questions.text: A team compares Row-based (TEXTFILE, Sequence) vs Column-based (ORC, Parquet) formats for an analytical workload that filters only 10 columns out of 140. Which is correct?
options: Row-based wins because it always reads fewer columns
Columnar wins because it reads only the columns referenced in the query, reducing I/O
Both perform identically — HDFS ignores file layout
Row-based formats are always smaller after compression
Columnar formats are not queryable from Hive
questions.shortExplanation: Columnar formats win for analytics because they read only the queried columns, cutting I/O.
questions.explanation: Analytical queries usually project just a few of the available columns. Row-based formats like TEXTFILE or Sequence store every row contiguously, so the engine must read all columns of every row even if it needs only a few. Columnar formats like ORC and Parquet store one column at a time on disk, so the engine can skip the columns the query does not need and read only the relevant ones, reducing I/O and improving compression at the same time. Row-based formats do not read fewer columns, performance is not identical between layouts, row-based compression is not always smaller, and columnar formats are fully Hive-queryable, so those claims are wrong.

questions.text: An architect compares Hadoop MapReduce vs Apache Spark for iterative anomaly-detection training. MapReduce writes intermediate results to HDFS between stages; Spark keeps intermediates in memory. What is the practical operational implication?
options: MapReduce incurs more I/O between stages because it materializes intermediate output to HDFS; Spark's in-memory model reduces I/O and accelerates iterative/multi-stage workloads
Spark cannot run on a Hadoop cluster
Both have identical I/O profiles
MapReduce keeps everything in memory; Spark writes to HDFS
Spark needs no scheduler and runs single-threaded only
questions.shortExplanation: MapReduce writes to HDFS between stages; Spark keeps intermediate data in memory, reducing I/O.
questions.explanation: Hadoop MapReduce serializes the output of every stage back to HDFS before the next stage reads it again, which causes heavy disk and network I/O, especially for iterative or multi-stage jobs. Spark keeps intermediate RDDs and DataFrames in memory across stages, so iterative workloads such as machine learning or graph algorithms run much faster. Spark can still spill to disk when memory is short, and it can read input from HDFS, but the in-memory pipeline is its key advantage. Saying Spark cannot run on Hadoop, that both have identical I/O, that MapReduce keeps everything in memory, or that Spark needs no scheduler all contradict how these engines actually work.
